Checking sRtr on your own SAFs

Source: vignettes/articles/checking-your-safs.Rmd
checking-your-safs.Rmd

sRtr’s automatic tests run on made-up data, because SRTR files cannot be shared. Real files differ from release to release: columns come and go, codes appear that no format lists, and identifiers that should match sometimes do not. Before you rely on sRtr for an analysis, run the checks below on your own standard analysis files (SAFs). Checks 1 to 4 take a few minutes in your usual R session. Check 5, the package’s own live tests, needs a copy of the source code and is worth running once per release. Together they tell you whether sRtr behaves on your release as it does on the releases it has been checked against. The checks cover the three kinds of data quality in a common framework: whether values conform to the documented formats, whether they are complete, and whether they are plausible (Kahn et al. 2016).

The code is not run on this website, because it needs real SAFs. It uses liver files; change the file keys for other organs.

Share counts only

The SRTR data use agreement does not allow sharing patient-level data. Everything below prints counts, never rows. Keep it that way if you change the code, so you can share the results, for example in a GitHub issue. The other sRtr articles that run on real files follow the same rules and link here.

  • Mask any count from 1 to 10. The helpers in the setup chunk print such a count as <11: mask_n() for counts you have computed, mask() for a frequency table of a column of categories, such as a status. Never use mask() on an identifier or a date: the table’s labels are the values themselves, so masking the counts hides nothing.
  • Do not share a total beside masked parts. If a table of a column shows every cell but one, together with the total, a reader recovers the masked cell by subtraction. Share the table or the total, not both, or check that no single masked cell can be worked out.
  • Do not share two counts that differ by a little. “1,204 registrations and 1,198 people” reveals 6. Print the difference instead, masked, or as a check that should be 0.
  • Summaries can describe a few people. A median or quartile of a small group is close to individual values. Look at such summaries yourself, and share them only when the group behind them is large.
  • Keep raw output on your computer. Test failures and warning messages can include exact counts and values from your files. Rewrite what they say in your own words, as in the example at the end of this article.

The first three rules follow the CMS cell size suppression policy: no count from 1 to 10, and none that can be worked out from other reported numbers (CMS 2020). The last two are sRtr’s own practice.

library(sRtr)
library(dplyr)

wd <- "path/to/your/SAFs"
set_srtr_wd(wd, release = "2303") # your release, named by year and month

mask_n <- function(n) {
  noquote(ifelse(n > 0 & n < 11, "<11", format(n, big.mark = ",")))
}
# For a column of categories only, never identifiers or dates.
mask <- function(x) mask_n(table(x, useNA = "ifany"))

1. Load with the warnings counted, not hidden

Loading a real file can give several warnings. Every sRtr warning has a class, so you can collect each kind instead of hiding them all with suppressWarnings():

seen <- list()
collect <- function(expr) {
  withCallingHandlers(
    expr,
    sRtr_warning = function(w) {
      kind <- class(w)[1]
      seen[[kind]] <<- c(seen[[kind]], conditionMessage(w))
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
}

tx <- collect(load_srtr_file("TX_LI"))
txf <- collect(load_srtr_file("TXF_LI"))

mask_n(lengths(seen))

The kinds you are most likely to see:

  • sRtr_warning_missing_columns or sRtr_warning_extra_columns: the file does not have the columns the dictionary lists for this release. A long list usually means the release is wrong (check set_srtr_wd(release =)); a short one may be a real difference worth reporting.
  • sRtr_warning_unknown_codes: values no format lists. sRtr keeps them as their own level, named <code>: not in format, and says which variable they are in. Some are known gaps in SRTR’s dictionary; a new one is worth reporting.
  • sRtr_warning_dictionary_gap: your release falls between the dictionary versions sRtr stores, and an entry differs between them.

To silence one kind in later code while keeping the others visible, muffle only that class, such as sRtr_warning_unknown_codes.

Read the messages in seen yourself, but do not share them as they are: some include exact row counts and the codes found.

2. Check the keys

Joins between SAF files rely on identifiers. These should hold, and anything else is worth knowing before you join:

mask_n(c(
  registrations = n_distinct(tx$TRR_ID, na.rm = TRUE),
  rows_beyond_one_per_registration =
    sum(!is.na(tx$TRR_ID)) - n_distinct(tx$TRR_ID, na.rm = TRUE),
  missing_trr_id = sum(is.na(tx$TRR_ID)),
  follow_up_registrations_not_in_tx =
    n_distinct(txf$TRR_ID[!is.na(txf$TRR_ID) & !txf$TRR_ID %in% tx$TRR_ID])
))

# Each registration belongs to one person. Check that first; only then is
# "registrations minus people" a count of repeat registrations.
ids <- tx |>
  filter(!is.na(TRR_ID), !is.na(PERS_ID)) |>
  distinct(TRR_ID, PERS_ID)
one_person_per_registration <- !anyDuplicated(ids$TRR_ID)
one_person_per_registration
if (one_person_per_registration) {
  mask_n(c(repeat_registrations = nrow(ids) - n_distinct(ids$PERS_ID)))
}
  • rows_beyond_one_per_registration should be 0: each row of a transplant file is one registration.
  • missing_trr_id should be 0.
  • one_person_per_registration should be TRUE. If it is not, that is worth reporting, and the next count is skipped.
  • repeat_registrations counts registrations after a person’s first one: people transplanted more than once have several registrations. It is not the number of people with a repeat transplant, nor all their registrations.
  • follow_up_registrations_not_in_tx should be 0: every follow-up form belongs to a registration in the transplant file.

Each difference is printed on its own, masked, rather than as two totals (see Share counts only).

For donors, a deceased donor file covers only deceased donors, so some transplant DONOR_IDs will not be in it:

donors <- collect(load_srtr_file("DONOR_DECEASED", col_select = "DONOR_ID"))
mask_n(c(
  donors_not_in_deceased_donors = n_distinct(
    tx$DONOR_ID[!is.na(tx$DONOR_ID) & !tx$DONOR_ID %in% donors$DONOR_ID]
  )
))

This counts distinct donors. One donor can give organs to several recipients, so it can be smaller than the number of transplants concerned.

3. Check labels 

unlabelled <- vapply(tx, \(x) is.null(attr(x, "label")), logical(1))
mask_n(c(columns = ncol(tx), without_a_label = sum(unlabelled)))

Almost every column should have a label, either the one stored in the SAS file or one from the dictionary.

4. Check that derived outcomes add up

Derived variables should be consistent with each other. These checks use the follow-up outcomes; the reasons behind them are in Follow-up forms are reports, not events and Follow-up windows and death.

tx <- add_txf_outcomes(tx)

# The status columns cover every registration once. Look at these tables
# yourself; shared beside the registration total, a table with a single
# masked cell gives that cell away.
mask(tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_STATUS)
mask(tx$FIRST_FU_REJ_STATUS)

# The last negative form always comes before the first report.
gap <- tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE - tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_LAST_NEG_DATE
mask_n(c(gaps = sum(!is.na(gap)), not_positive = sum(gap <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)))

not_positive should be 0. The merge report attached by add_txf_outcomes() should agree with the status columns: registrations with forms plus those with no follow-up make up all registrations. The report counts distinct registrations, so count those on the other side too, and print only whether they agree:

report <- attr(tx, "txf_report")
no_follow_up <- n_distinct(
  tx$TRR_ID[!is.na(tx$TRR_ID) & tx$FIRST_FU_MALIG_STATUS == "no follow-up"]
)
report$registrations == report$registrations_with_forms + no_follow_up

This should be TRUE.

The time-to-event outcomes come from add_time_to_event_outcomes():

out <- collect(add_time_to_event_outcomes(tx))

# The date a counted event is timed at is the _CENSOR column, not
# FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE, which keeps the first report of all for auditing.
counted <- out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_BINARY %in% 1L
event <- out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_CENSOR
lafu <- out$TFL_LAFUDATE
death <- out$REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE
# The window ends at last follow-up, or at death if that is earlier. With
# no last follow-up date, the end is unknown: death is not used instead.
end <- if_else(!is.na(death) & death < lafu, death, lafu)
dated <- counted & !is.na(event)

mask_n(c(
  before_transplant = sum(dated & event < out$REC_TX_DT, na.rm = TRUE),
  after_window_end = sum(dated & event > end, na.rm = TRUE),
  with_no_last_follow_up = sum(dated & is.na(lafu)),
  counted_but_undated = sum(counted & is.na(event))
))

The first three should be 0. counted_but_undated is the events reported only on undated forms: they count, with an unknown time.

5. Run the package’s live tests

sRtr’s test suite includes live tests that run only on real files. They check, among other things, that columns load with the right types, that codes match the dictionary, and that derived outcomes are consistent. The tests are not installed with the package, so you need a copy of the source that matches the version you have installed:

# The commit your installed copy was built from, if installed from GitHub:
packageDescription("sRtr")$RemoteSha

Clone the repository and check out that commit. In a terminal:

git clone https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr
git -C sRtr checkout <commit>

Then start a fresh R session, so the tests run against the version you checked out, run the setup chunk at the top of this article again (it sets wd and the masking helpers), and run the tests:

Sys.setenv(
  SRTR_LIVE_TESTS = "true",
  SRTR_WD = wd,
  SRTR_RELEASE = "2303"
)
testthat::test_local(
  "path/to/the/sRtr/clone",
  reporter = "summary",
  stop_on_failure = FALSE
)

Each live test names the files it needs and skips when your folder does not have them, so you can run the whole suite with whatever files you have. To run one area, add filter, such as filter = "add_txf_outcomes". A failure means sRtr does something on your release that it has not been checked for. Please report it (see below). The test output itself stays on your computer: a failure message can print values from your files.

6. Report what you find

If a live test fails, a check above gives an unexpected answer, or a warning lists something new, please open an issue at https://github.com/VagishHemmige/sRtr/issues. Write it from the pieces below, not by pasting output: test output and warning messages can include exact counts and values from your files.

  • the SAF release, and which files you used;
  • packageDescription("sRtr")$RemoteSha and your R version;
  • the name of the failing test, or the warning’s class (such as sRtr_warning_unknown_codes);
  • the file key and column name;
  • a masked count from mask_n(), if a count helps.

For example: “Release 2303, TX_LI. sRtr_warning_unknown_codes for REC_COD: <11 rows with codes not in the format.” Never attach SAF files, rows from them, or unmasked counts.
